passage: The steel box of laddoos sat on the top shelf of the Pune flat. Chinmayi, five, had already eaten one after dinner. "One more, Papa!" Her father, Mridul, shook his head and closed the lid. Her face went red before she said a single word. Her feet stamped on the tiles, once, twice, hard. "I hate you!" she shouted, fists tight. "It's not fair! You always say no!" She threw herself onto the sofa cushion, kicking. Mridul stood still, the box in his hand, while the shouting filled the small room.

qa.q: Where was the box of laddoos kept?
qa.a: The steel box of laddoos sat on the top shelf of the Pune flat.

qa.q: What was Chinmayi feeling when her father closed the lid, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt it was deeply unfair and was furious 😠; her face went red and her feet stamped before any words came, then she shouted "It's not fair!"

qa.q: At this early moment, what could Mridul do that might help the evening turn toward calm?
qa.a: He could stay near her, name the anger in a quiet voice and keep the answer the same, so she learns that big feelings are safe but the limit holds.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridul to hear "I hate you" from his five-year-old?
qa.a: It probably stings even if he knows she doesn't mean it, and he may feel torn between comforting her and giving in just to stop the noise.

grounding: Shows a five-year-old girl refused a second sweet whose body erupts in stamping and shouting "I hate you" before calmer words come.

passage:
"Mumma, can I have another toffee?"
"You had one after lunch, Nandini. That's it for today."
"Just one small one!"
"No, sweetheart. The jar is closed now."
Nandini's chin wobbled. Her feet began to stamp on the floor, harder and harder.
"No! No! It's not fair!"
"I know you really wanted it."
"I hate you! I hate you, Mumma!"
Sunaina put the jar on top of the fridge and knelt down. "You're very cross."
"Go away!" Nandini shouted, stamping again, her cheeks wet and hot.

qa.q: Where did Sunaina put the jar?
qa.a: Sunaina put the jar on top of the fridge.

qa.q: Why did Nandini shout "I hate you" at her mother?
qa.a: She wanted the toffee badly and the no felt unfair; the anger hit her body first, so her feet stamped and the hurtful words burst out before calmer ones could.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Sunaina in this moment?
qa.a: She can keep the jar closed, stay close and name the anger calmly, which shows Nandini that the feeling is allowed but shouting will not change the answer.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel hearing "Go away!" right after she knelt down?
qa.a: She may feel pushed away and a little hurt, yet understand that Nandini is overwhelmed, so she might wait nearby rather than leave.

grounding: Illustrates a five-year-old girl denied a second sweet, stamping and shouting "I hate you" as her body reacts before reasoning.

passage:
Nitin, notes for tomorrow when you babysit Juhi.
Today at the park she asked for a second ice lolly. I said no.
First came crying, big tears, peeking at me between sobs.
Then promises: "I'll sleep early, I'll eat all my dal, pinky promise!"
When that didn't work, she shouted so loudly the whole bench turned around.
Each time she stopped and checked my face.
I nearly caved at the shouting part. I didn't.
If she gets the lolly after screaming, tomorrow she'll scream sooner.
So please: kind voice, same answer. 🙏
- Varun

qa.q: What did Juhi promise when the crying didn't work?
qa.a: She promised, "I'll sleep early, I'll eat all my dal, pinky promise!"

qa.q: Why did Juhi keep stopping to check Varun's face?
qa.a: Juhi was hopeful the no might move; each pause shows her watching to see if crying, promising or shouting was starting to work.

qa.q: What turning point does Varun's note point to at this stage?
qa.a: Keeping the same answer even through the loudest shouting, so Juhi learns that tantrums don't shift limits and the pattern fades instead of growing.

qa.q: What would tomorrow be like for Nitin if he hands Juhi a lolly after a scream?
qa.a: Nitin would get a quick moment of quiet, but Juhi would learn that screaming works and try it sooner and louder, making the day harder.

grounding: A caregiver's note records a five-year-old girl moving from crying to promising to shouting while watching whether the limit will move.

passage: The weekly haat at Rangpo was loud with bargaining. Pema, five, stopped at a stall of tin whistles. "Papa, buy one!" Her father, Varun, said, "Not today, we came for rice." Pema's lip trembled and she cried loudly, one eye open, watching him. He kept walking. She ran after him. "I'll carry the bag! I'll never ask again!" He shook his head gently. Then she stood in the mud and shouted, so loudly the vegetable seller laughed. Varun felt every face turn. His hand went to his pocket, then stopped. "Still no, Pema," he said, and held out his hand.

qa.q: What had Pema and Varun come to the haat to buy?
qa.a: They came for rice.

qa.q: What does Pema crying with one eye open suggest about what she wants?
qa.a: She wants the tin whistle and is checking whether her tears are moving her father; the crying is partly a test of the limit, not only sadness.

qa.q: What is the turning point in this scene, and why does it matter?
qa.a: It is the moment Varun's hand goes to his pocket and stops; by holding the no through the shouting, he keeps Pema from learning that a louder tantrum wins.

qa.q: What is Varun going through as the vegetable seller laughs?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed with every face turned his way and tempted to buy the whistle just to end it, which makes staying calm harder.

grounding: Shows a young girl trying crying, promising and then shouting while testing whether her father's no will give way.

passage: Alka was rolling rotis when Bhupen came home from the rice mill, dust in his hair. Their daughter Mamoni, five, wanted another piece of gur. He said no. "I hate you, Deuta!" she screamed. Alka saw his jaw go tight. He took a step, his voice already rising: "Say that again and..." Then he stopped. Alka watched him put both hands on the doorframe and let out one long breath, then another. His shoulders came down. When he turned back to Mamoni, his voice was low. Alka went on rolling, quietly relieved.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen come home from?
qa.a: Bhupen came home from the rice mill.

qa.q: How can Alka tell that Bhupen felt stung by Mamoni's words?
qa.a: His jaw went tight, he took a step and his voice started rising, which shows the words hit him hard after a long day.

qa.q: What was the key moment that changed how the evening could go?
qa.a: Bhupen stopping mid-sentence, holding the doorframe and breathing out twice; noticing his own heat let him answer Mamoni in a low voice instead of punishing her.

qa.q: What might Mamoni have felt if her father had finished that angry sentence?
qa.a: She would likely have felt frightened and even more upset, and the evening could have turned into a shouting match instead of a limit she could slowly accept.

grounding: A mother watches her tired husband feel stung by "I hate you", start to punish, and then catch his own heat and breathe first.

passage: Clara was drying dishes in her son's kitchen in Lisbon when Mateo got back from his late shift at the tram depot. Rosa, five, was meant to be heading for bath and bed, but she wanted another biscuit. "No, querida." "I hate you! You're the worst papa!" Clara saw Mateo's face flush. He opened his mouth wide, as if to shout louder than Rosa. Then he closed it, pressed his palms together and breathed out slowly through his nose. "I'm tired and cross," he said quietly, mostly to himself. Clara put the towel down and smiled at him.

qa.q: Where had Mateo worked his late shift?
qa.a: He had worked his late shift at the tram depot.

qa.q: What does Mateo saying "I'm tired and cross" to himself suggest about his state?
qa.a: It suggests he noticed his own anger and exhaustion rising and named it, which helped him not match Rosa's shouting.

qa.q: Which small action gave Mateo a turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Pressing his palms together and breathing out slowly gave him a pause, so the urge to shout louder could pass before he answered Rosa.

qa.q: How does Clara see what her son did?
qa.a: She seems proud and relieved 🙂; putting the towel down and smiling suggests she knows how hard it is to hold back after a long shift.

grounding: A grandmother observes a tired father stung by his daughter's "I hate you", tempted to out-shout her, who notices his heat and breathes.

passage: The rasgulla tin was nearly empty on the kitchen counter of their Kolkata flat. Pallavi, five, lay on the floor kicking. "One more! Give it!" Her father, Uday, sat down on the floor beside her, not too close. "You're really angry, I can see that," he said evenly. "And no more sweets today." "You're mean!" He didn't answer that. He didn't call her a baby, and he didn't offer a biscuit instead. He just stayed. "When you want a hug, I'm right here." Pallavi kicked twice more, then slower.

qa.q: What did Uday say he would be there for?
qa.a: He said, "When you want a hug, I'm right here."

qa.q: Why might Pallavi's kicks be slowing at the end?
qa.a: His steady voice and staying close may be helping her feel safe enough to let the anger drain, even though she still wants the sweet.

qa.q: What makes Uday's response a turning point in the tantrum?
qa.a: He names her anger and keeps the no without shaming, bribing or shouting, and he stays available, so the storm can pass without the limit moving.

qa.q: What is Pallavi experiencing now that the limit isn't moving?
qa.a: She is still angry and calling him mean, but she is also finding out that her father stays near her even when she is at her worst.

grounding: Shows a father acknowledging his daughter's anger, holding the no on sweets without shame or bargaining, and staying available for comfort.

passage:
"I want more cake! Now!"
"You're so angry, Aadya. I hear it." Mridul crouched to her height.
"Give me Eshaan's piece then!"
"No more sweets today. That's the answer."
"You're a bad papa!"
Eshaan, nine, snorted. "She's being a baby."
"Eshaan, no names, please." Mridul turned back. "Still no cake, beta. I'm not cross with you."
Aadya howled and threw a cushion.
"I'll sit right here," he said, settling on the rug. "Come when you're ready."
The cushion landed near his knee. He left it there.

qa.q: How old is Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan is nine.

qa.q: What did Aadya want when she asked for Eshaan's piece?
qa.a: She was hoping to find a way around the no, trying a different route to get cake while she was still furious.

qa.q: How does Mridul handle Eshaan's comment, and why does it matter here?
qa.a: He stops the name-calling at once, so Aadya is not shamed while he holds the limit, keeping the focus on calm firmness.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be feeling while his sister howls?
qa.a: He may be irritated by the noise and protective of his own cake, and hearing Papa stop the name-calling shows him how anger is handled at home.

grounding: A father names his daughter's anger, keeps the no on sweets, blocks shaming, and waits nearby for her to come to him.

passage: The crying had gone quiet in the flat in Buenos Aires. Valentina, five, peeped out from behind the curtain. Her papá, Andrés, was on the sofa folding laundry, not looking cross. Her throat still hurt from yelling at him about the dulce de leche. She shuffled over, stopped, then climbed into his lap and hid her face in his shirt. "I said bad words," she whispered. Andrés wrapped both arms around her. "You were very angry. I still love you, all the way." Valentina's body went soft and heavy. She kept her face hidden, but she held on.

qa.q: What was Andrés doing on the sofa?
qa.a: He was on the sofa folding laundry, not looking cross.

qa.q: What does Valentina hiding her face in his shirt suggest she feels?
qa.a: She seems ashamed of the bad words and relieved to be held 🤍; hiding her face shows the shame, while holding on shows she needs to know they're still close.

qa.q: What did Andrés say that helped at this stage, and why?
qa.a: He named her anger and said he still loved her "all the way", which tells her the bond survived her outburst.

qa.q: What might Andrés be feeling as Valentina climbs into his lap?
qa.a: He is probably relieved the storm has passed and tender toward her, glad she came back to him on her own.

grounding: After crying, a five-year-old girl climbs into her father's lap, ashamed and relieved, and hears that her anger did not make her unlovable.

passage: The community centre hall smelled of floor polish after dance class. Preeti, five, had wailed by the shoe rack because her father said no to a second laddoo from the snack table. Now she sat on the bench, hiccupping. Jagdish sat at the far end, waiting. Slowly Preeti slid along the bench, bit by bit, until she was against his arm. Then she crawled into his lap. "Are you still my papa?" she mumbled into his kurta. "Always," Jagdish said, rocking her a little. "Even when you're angry." Her fingers curled into his sleeve.

qa.q: Where had Preeti wailed?
qa.a: Preeti had wailed by the shoe rack.

qa.q: What worry is behind Preeti's question "Are you still my papa?"
qa.a: She seems afraid that her anger may have broken their closeness, so she needs to hear she is still loved.

qa.q: Why was waiting at the far end of the bench a good choice for Jagdish?
qa.a: It let Preeti cool down at her own pace and come to him when ready, so the reconnection felt safe and was her own choice.

qa.q: What might Jagdish feel as her fingers curl into his sleeve?
qa.a: Likely relief and warmth, knowing the hard moment is over and his daughter still trusts him.

grounding: A young girl, after a tantrum over a sweet, slides into her father's lap needing to know that her anger has not broken the bond.

passage: I'm Zeenat, and I was doing homework at the table when it happened. Earlier Ammi had raised her voice at my little sister Dilnaz over the biscuit fight. At bedtime I saw Ammi sit on Dilnaz's bed. "I shouted today. I'm sorry. That wasn't kind of me." Dilnaz just nodded. Then they made a list with crayons: stomp like a soft cat, draw an angry picture, ask for a squeeze. Dilnaz practised the cat stomp, giggling. I can't say what was in her head, but she taped the list to the wall herself.

qa.q: What three ideas did Ammi and Dilnaz put on the list?
qa.a: Stomp like a soft cat, draw an angry picture, and ask for a squeeze.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz taping the list to the wall herself suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels some ownership of the plan and maybe pride, though Zeenat admits she can't be sure what was in her head.

qa.q: Why did Ammi's apology matter at this stage?
qa.a: By saying sorry for shouting, Ammi showed that grown-ups also make things right, which makes it easier for Dilnaz to repair after her own anger.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see the bedtime talk?
qa.a: She watches from the homework table as an outsider, noticing her sister's nod and giggle, and seems quietly glad the fight ended this way. 😊

grounding: An older sister watches a mother apologise for shouting and make a list of calm anger choices with a five-year-old.

passage:
Monday: Suraj flung his shoe after Papa said no to more jalebi. Naveen snapped, "Stop it!" louder than he meant.
Wednesday: At bedtime Naveen said, "I yelled on Monday. I'm sorry." Together they drew three pictures: soft stomping feet, a crayon scribble, two arms for a hug. Suraj stuck them on the fridge.
Saturday: Told no to a second ice cream, Suraj's face crumpled. He marched to the fridge, stomped softly, grabbed a crayon and scribbled hard. Then he walked over with his arms up. Naveen lifted him. "You used your plan," he whispered.

qa.q: What did Suraj do with the three pictures?
qa.a: Suraj stuck them on the fridge.

qa.q: What does Suraj walking over with his arms up on Saturday suggest he wanted?
qa.a: He wanted comfort after his anger and trusted that asking for a hug would be welcomed, just as the plan said.

qa.q: Which step on Wednesday set up Saturday's calmer moment?
qa.a: Naveen's apology plus drawing the three choices together gave Suraj concrete things to do with anger, and he remembered them days later.

qa.q: What might Naveen feel when Suraj uses the plan on Saturday?
qa.a: He likely feels proud and relieved, seeing that the talk after his own mistake helped his son handle a no better.

grounding: Across several days a father apologises for yelling and practises stomping, drawing and hugging with his son, who later uses the plan.

passage:
Tuesday. In Class 9 science, Manoj sir noticed the boy in the third row again. Dhruv never raised his hand in the loud rush of answers, but when the room emptied he asked quietly, "Sir, if plants make food from light, what happens in a cave?" Manoj wrote the question in his diary.
Friday. Manoj left a library book on Dhruv's desk: a thin book on cave life, with a slip that said, "For your cave question. No test on this."
The next Thursday. Dhruv came up after class holding the book, ears pink. "Sir, I finished it. Can I ask about page forty?" Manoj pulled up a chair. Dhruv, who usually looked at the floor, looked straight at him while he talked.

qa.q: What did the slip in the book say?
qa.a: The slip said, "For your cave question. No test on this."

qa.q: What do Dhruv's pink ears and steady gaze suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seems surprised and a little shy at being noticed, but also encouraged; looking straight at Manoj sir shows he felt taken seriously.

qa.q: What made Manoj sir's offer a good first step toward mentoring?
qa.a: It was small and pressure-free, a book tied to Dhruv's own question with no test, so a quiet student could accept it without feeling put on the spot.

qa.q: What is it like for Dhruv to be singled out by a teacher this way?
qa.a: It is likely surprising and quietly powerful: an adult outside his family has noticed his thinking, which may make him braver about asking more.

grounding: Over a week a science teacher notices a quiet boy's careful question, offers extra reading, and sees the student light up at being noticed.

passage: Farhan, you're new here, so let me, Ganga, tell you about Chhaya. Twenty years back she sat at the last bench in my Class 10 chemistry and never spoke. But her test papers had tiny pencil questions in the margins: 'Why does iron rust and flake but copper only turns green?' I nearly missed them. One evening I stayed late, wrote an answer under each question, and gave her an old college book on metals. She stared at me like I'd grown two heads. The next week the margins were full again. She works with metals now. So check the margins of the quiet ones. That's where they hide.

qa.q: Where did Chhaya write her questions?
qa.a: Chhaya wrote tiny pencil questions in the margins of her test papers.

qa.q: What does Chhaya's stare suggest about how she felt at being noticed?
qa.a: She seems startled that a teacher had read and answered her quiet questions; the surprise hints that no teacher had done that for her before.

qa.q: What advice does Ganga pass on, and why is it useful for a new teacher?
qa.a: To check the margins of quiet students, because careful thinkers who don't speak up often show their curiosity in small, easy-to-miss ways.

qa.q: How might Farhan's classes change if Farhan follows Ganga's advice?
qa.a: Farhan might spot quiet students' questions early and offer extra reading, giving some of them the same lift Chhaya got.

grounding: A senior teacher recalls noticing a silent student's careful science questions and offering extra reading, which surprised and encouraged her.

passage: The school bus had already left the kasba square when Kiran hovered by the staffroom door, dupatta twisted around one finger. Salma ma'am was marking copies. "Ma'am... can I ask something? You won't laugh?" "Sit." Kiran sat on the edge of the chair. "Everyone says I should be a doctor because I got good marks. But I feel dizzy when I see blood. Is that stupid?" She watched Salma ma'am's mouth for a smile. None came. "It's a real question. What part of medicine pulls you, and what part scares you?" Kiran's shoulders dropped an inch. "The part where you work out what's wrong," she said, and pulled the chair closer.

qa.q: What was Kiran twisting around one finger?
qa.a: Kiran had her dupatta twisted around one finger.

qa.q: Why did Kiran watch Salma ma'am's mouth for a smile?
qa.a: She was afraid her doubt would be laughed at 😰, so she was testing whether the teacher would take her seriously.

qa.q: What turning point does Salma ma'am offer at this stage, and how?
qa.a: By calling it a real question and asking what pulls and scares her, she treats Kiran's doubt with respect, which invites her to open up further.

qa.q: What might Salma ma'am be noticing as Kiran pulls the chair closer?
qa.a: Likely that Kiran's guard is dropping and trust is beginning, and that this student has thought carefully about her future.

grounding: A teenage girl brings her doubts about becoming a doctor to a teacher, tests for mockery, and relaxes when met with respect.

passage: Rain streaked the windows of the biology lab in Toronto. Rania lingered after the others left, pretending to wipe a bench that was already clean. Ms Jin looked up from her laptop. "Something on your mind?" "Kind of." Rania laughed, too quickly. "My parents think I'm going to med school. I'm not sure I even want to. Probably sounds dumb." "It doesn't." Ms Jin closed the laptop. "Tell me what you're not sure about." Rania talked for a minute, then stopped, checking her face. Ms Jin only nodded and waited. So Rania kept going, and this time she sat down.

qa.q: What was Rania pretending to do after class?
qa.a: She was pretending to wipe a bench that was already clean.

qa.q: What does Rania's quick laugh and "Probably sounds dumb" suggest?
qa.a: She is nervous about being judged and protects herself by mocking her own doubt before anyone else can.

qa.q: Which small move by Ms Jin lowered Rania's guard?
qa.a: Closing the laptop and asking what she wasn't sure about showed full attention and respect, so Rania felt safe to keep talking and sit down.

qa.q: If Ms Jin had joked about it, what would change for Rania?
qa.a: She would probably have left quickly and kept her doubts private, missing the chance to think them through with an adult she trusts.

grounding: A teenage girl tests whether her teacher will take her doubts about medicine seriously, and each respectful reply lowers her guard.

passage: Neelam, don't laugh, okay? You know Rawat sir, the new history teacher? He says 'Let's question the source' before every lesson, and now I say it too. I said it at dinner! Papa asked what I meant and I just repeated sir's line. I've started reading everything he mentions. Three books this month, me, Gargi, who used to sleep in history! But yesterday sir said village farming never changed for centuries, and I wrote it down like scripture. Then you showed me that chapter saying it did. I felt weird. Like, can sir be wrong? Of course he can. It just never crossed my mind.

qa.q: How many books has Gargi read this month?
qa.a: Three books this month.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when Neelam showed her the chapter?
qa.a: She felt weird and unsettled, because she had never imagined Rawat sir could be wrong and had treated his words like scripture.

qa.q: What could help Gargi at this stage of admiring her mentor?
qa.a: She could keep the reading habit sir sparked while checking his claims against other sources, and even ask him about the chapter, so admiration feeds her own judgement.

qa.q: How might Neelam see Gargi's new way of talking?
qa.a: Neelam may find it funny and a bit worrying, glad Gargi loves history now but noticing she repeats sir's lines instead of her own thoughts.

grounding: A teenage girl describes copying her male teacher's phrases and treating his views as truth, until a wrong claim shows his limits.

passage: I'm Sahil, Dolma's classmate, and I've watched her change since Mr Chettri took over debate club. She used to argue with everyone. Now she starts sentences with 'As Mr Chettri says.' When Karma questioned one of his rules in practice, Dolma snapped, 'He's been doing this for twenty years.' She carries his marked-up notes around like certificates. Her speeches are sharper, honestly, and she won the district round. But at lunch I asked what she thought about school uniforms, and she said, 'I'll ask him.' I don't know if she noticed how that sounded. I did.

qa.q: What did Dolma win?
qa.a: She won the district round.

qa.q: What might Dolma's snapping at Karma show about how she sees Mr Chettri?
qa.a: It suggests she admires him so much that questioning him feels like an attack, as if his view must be the truth.

qa.q: What could Mr Chettri do to support Dolma's growth at this stage?
qa.a: He could invite disagreement in practice and ask Dolma for her own opinion before sharing his, so her admiration turns into independent thinking.

qa.q: How does Sahil feel about the change in Dolma?
qa.a: He sees real gains, like sharper speeches and a win, but is uneasy 🤔 that she no longer seems to trust her own opinions.

grounding: A classmate observes a teenage girl adopting her male coach's phrases and opinions, growing in skill while losing her own judgement.

passage: The science exhibition was the next morning, and the power had just gone out in the school lab. By the light of her phone torch, Baljeet held up her water-filter model for Kiran ma'am. "The sand layer is in the wrong order," ma'am said flatly. "And your chart claims it makes water safe to drink. You haven't tested that. A judge will catch it in ten seconds." Baljeet's face went hot. She'd spent three weekends on it. "You could have said something nice first," she muttered, jaw tight. Kiran ma'am didn't flinch. "I'm saying this because you're capable of first prize. Come, we'll fix the layers together before the lights come back." Baljeet stood stiffly for a moment, then picked up the gravel.

qa.q: What was wrong with the sand layer?
qa.a: The sand layer was in the wrong order.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet mutter "You could have said something nice first"?
qa.a: She felt stung and angry after three weekends of work, and the flat words hurt more because they came the night before the exhibition.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Baljeet in this moment?
qa.a: Picking up the gravel and fixing the layers with Kiran ma'am turns the sting into improvement, letting her see the critique as help from someone who believes in her.

qa.q: How might Kiran ma'am feel when Baljeet mutters at her?
qa.a: She may feel a flicker of discomfort but stays steady, because she cares more about Baljeet doing her best than about being liked in that moment.

grounding: Under time pressure a teacher bluntly critiques a teenage girl's project; she feels stung and angry, then accepts the warm, high-standard help.

passage: Vidya had edited her short film until two a.m., and now it played on the classroom projector in their Bengaluru school. When the lights came on, Pranav sir leaned back. "The shots are lovely. The story isn't there yet. Your ending tells me what to feel instead of showing me. And the middle drags by a full minute." A couple of classmates shifted in their seats. Vidya stared at her notebook, cheeks burning. Who asked him? she thought, and then, unfairly, that he'd never liked her work. After class he stopped by her desk. "I wouldn't bother if I didn't think it could be great. Cut the minute and show me the ending. I'll watch it again Friday." Vidya nodded without looking up, but she opened her laptop on the bus home.

qa.q: How long did Pranav sir say the middle dragged?
qa.a: The middle drags by a full minute.

qa.q: What was Vidya thinking when the lights came on and her cheeks burned?
qa.a: She was stung and briefly angry, thinking "Who asked him?" and unfairly deciding he'd never liked her work.

qa.q: What did Pranav sir do that turned harsh feedback into mentoring?
qa.a: He followed the blunt critique with warmth after class, saying he believed the film could be great and offering to watch it again on Friday.

qa.q: What might Pranav sir experience as Vidya nods without looking up?
qa.a: He may be unsure how his words landed and hope she can see past the sting, trusting that his high standards come from care.

grounding: A teacher gives a teenage girl blunt feedback on her film; she feels stung and angry, but his warm follow-up shows the critique as care.
